name: Airtable
summary: A database that looks like a spreadsheet: typed fields, linked records, views, forms and automations, with small applications built on top in Interfaces.

factors: Formulas, rollups and lookups are Airtable's own and have no equivalent elsewhere
Interfaces and automations are rebuilt from nothing anywhere else: there is no format to carry them in
Attachments sit on Airtable's storage behind URLs that stop working hours after an export
Colleagues' bookmarked views, embedded forms and shared links all break on the same day
Scripting extensions and API calls get woven into other teams' workflows, often without anyone recording where

export.summary: A view exports to CSV in one click and the API returns full records as JSON, so getting the values out is not the problem. What does not come out is the structure: field types, relationships, formulas, views, forms, automations and Interfaces.

methods.name: CSV per view
methods.detail: Download a table as CSV from a grid view. Hidden fields are left out, so make every field visible first. There is no single action that exports a whole base.

methods.name: REST API
methods.detail: Fetch records, field types and table structure as JSON. This is the only way to capture a base's schema, and it needs a personal access token and a script.

methods.name: Base snapshots and duplication
methods.detail: Snapshots and duplicates restore a base inside Airtable. They are useful before a migration and are not a portable export.

caveats: Attachment URLs in an export expire within a few hours: download the files straight away or they are gone
Formulas, rollups and lookups export as the values they currently show, not as formulas
Linked records export as record names, so relationships have to be matched up again on the other side
Record comments, field descriptions and anything held in extensions are not in a CSV export
Interfaces, automations, view filters and colour rules are not exported in any format

paths.verdict: The shortest move if you want the interface to stay familiar, since Baserow keeps Airtable's shape closely. Check which views and permissions you need first: several of them are paid tiers.

import.summary: Baserow imports a base from an Airtable public share link, bringing tables, fields, rows and files, and writes a report table listing what it could not map. Field types that have no equivalent arrive as text, so check them afterwards.

links.label: Import an Airtable base into Baserow

transfers: Tables, fields and rows from a share link
Attachments, unless you skip files to speed the import up
Grid views and the basics of their configuration
lost: Automations, which have to be rebuilt as Baserow automations or webhooks
Interfaces: there is no equivalent to import into
Formulas, rollups and lookups, which need rewriting as Baserow formula fields
Kanban, calendar and timeline views unless you pay for premium

paths.verdict: The better destination if your base is really a relational spreadsheet, or if you need row-level access control. The data comes over intact; the work is rewriting formulas in Python and rebuilding anything you had in Interfaces.

import.summary: Grist connects to Airtable and imports a base table by table, keeping attachments and the references between tables rather than flattening them to names. Linked record fields become Reference columns and Airtable's select colours map to Grist choices. Formula columns are not translated: they arrive as comments on the column, which is the text you work from when rewriting them in Python. On a self-hosted instance the connector has to be switched on with OAuth credentials first, or you use a personal access token.

transfers: Tables, fields and rows, with field types mapped rather than guessed
References between tables, as Reference and Reference List columns
Attachments, pulled across by the importer
Choice fields, with their Airtable colours
lost: Formulas, rollups and lookups: the expression arrives as a column comment and is rewritten in Python
Views, forms and Interfaces, which the importer does not cover
Automations, which have no equivalent in the open-source core
